correctness.rationale: A total dominating set covers every one-dimensional subspace and therefore covers the entire vector space, giving the known lower bound \(q+1\). A hyperplane pencil through a codimension-two subspace is a \(q+1\)-clique covering the space, so equality holds. For an arbitrary \(q+1\)-cover, enlarge members to hyperplanes. No duplicate can occur, because then at most \(q\) proper subspaces would cover the space. Relative to one hyperplane, the other \(q\) outside pieces each have exactly \(q^{n-2}(q-1)\) vectors and their total cardinality equals the full complement, so they are pairwise disjoint; hence all pairwise hyperplane intersections coincide in one codimension-two subspace. The original subspaces must equal those hyperplanes because each uniquely owns its outside piece. The Gaussian count follows from choosing the common codimension-two subspace. For odd \(q\), the even clique pencil has a perfect matching; for even \(q\), parity forces one extra vertex and adding a nonzero line in the common core gives a matching. The actual frozen verifier was read and its representative finite-field enumerations agree with the proof.
correctness.risk: The proof is uniform for all prime powers; finite verifier cases are corroborative only.

value.rationale: The result upgrades a known numerical ordinary-domination threshold to a complete geometric classification of every minimum total set, counts all minimizers, and settles paired domination with a parity boundary. The codimension-two pencil is a natural finite-projective structure rather than an arbitrary parameter slice.
value.risk: The principal contribution is the equality structure and paired refinement rather than a new cover-number threshold.

final_claim: For the intersection graph of proper nonzero subspaces of an \(n\)-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb F_q\), with \(n\ge3\), the total domination number is \(q+1\); every minimum total dominating set is exactly the pencil of all \(q+1\) hyperplanes through one codimension-two subspace; there are \(\begin{bmatrix}n\\2\end{bmatrix}_q\) such sets; and paired domination is \(q+1\) for odd \(q\) and \(q+2\) for even \(q\).
limitations: Dimension at least three; dimension two has an edgeless intersection graph.
For even \(q\), the minimum paired-domination number is determined but all minimum paired sets are not classified.
